q: Physics, like any other branch of science, is based on systematic observations and precise _____.
e: Physics, like any other branch of science, is based on systematic observations and precise measurements. Measurements here means a comparison with an agreed standard that gives you a number. Calculations: arithmetic you do after the data exist.

q: Most experiments in Physics require the observations made to be _____ rather than qualitative.
e: Most experiments in Physics require the observations made to be quantitative rather than qualitative. Quantitative here means observations written as numbers, not just hot or cold. Theoretical: on paper, without the measured numbers this experiment needs.

q: A standard quantity of some kind, referred to as a _____, is first established.
e: A standard quantity of some kind, referred to as a unit, is first established. Unit here means an agreed amount you use as the scale of a measurement. Constant: a quantity that does not change, not the agreed measuring unit.

q: A _____ is something or a reference used as a measure for length, mass and time.
e: A standard is something or a reference used as a measure for length, mass and time. Standard here means the reference you compare length, mass, or time against. Unit: an agreed amount you use as the scale of a measurement.

q: A _____ is a quantity or an amount used as a standard of measurement.
e: A unit is a quantity or an amount used as a standard of measurement. Unit here means an agreed amount you use as the scale of a measurement.

q: A physical quantity is the quantity that can be measured, and consists of a numerical magnitude and a _____.
e: A physical quantity is the quantity that can be measured, and consists of a numerical magnitude and a unit. Unit here means an agreed amount you use as the scale of a measurement involving that.

q: A physical quantity can be expressed as $Q=Nu$, where $N$ is a _____.
e: A physical quantity can be expressed as $Q=Nu$, where $N$ is a dimensionless number. The physics in this sentence is built around dimensionless number. Derived unit: an agreed amount you use as the scale of a measurement.

q: In the expression $Q=Nu$ for a physical quantity, the symbol $u$ represents the _____.
e: In the expression $Q=Nu$ for a physical quantity, the symbol $u$ represents the unit. Unit here means an agreed amount you use as the scale of a measurement.

q: Physical quantities can be classified as the basic type and the _____ type.
e: Physical quantities can be classified as the basic type and the derived type. The physics in this sentence is built around derived involving basic.

q: Length, mass, time, temperature, electric current, amount of substance, and luminous intensity are classified as _____ physical quantities.
e: Length, mass, time, temperature, electric current, amount of substance, and luminous intensity are classified as basic physical quantities. Current is charge passing a point per second.

q: Area, volume, velocity, work, and energy are classified as _____ physical quantities.
e: Area, volume, velocity, work, and energy are classified as derived physical quantities. Velocity is directed. Speed is the size of that velocity.

q: A _____ unit is a unit of measurement formed by combining the basic (or base) units of a system.
e: A derived unit is a unit of measurement formed by combining the basic (or base) units of a system. You compare the unknown amount with a standard so the result is a number with a unit. Standard: the reference you compare length, mass, or time against.

q: The base unit of distance is 'm' and that of time is 's', therefore the unit of speed is _____.
e: The base unit of distance is 'm' and that of time is 's', therefore the unit of speed is $\text{m s}^{-1}$. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: The British system is based on foot (ft), pound (lb) and second (s) and is therefore also called the _____ system.
e: The British system is based on foot (ft), pound (lb) and second (s) and is therefore also called the FPS system. FPS names the British system is based on foot (ft), pound (lb) and second (s) and is therefore also called the system involving foot.

q: The metric system consists of the CGS system and the _____ system.
e: The metric system consists of the CGS system and the MKS system. The physics in this sentence is built around MKS involving system.

q: The CGS system is based on centimetre (cm), gram (g) and _____.
e: The CGS system is based on centimetre (cm), gram (g) and second (s). The physics in this sentence is built around second (s).

q: The MKS system is based on metre (m), kilogram (kg) and _____.
e: The MKS system is based on metre (m), kilogram (kg) and ampere (A). Current is charge passing a point per second.

q: The SI unit is just the modified form of the _____ system of units.
e: The SI unit is just the modified form of the MKS system of units. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit involving form.

q: In 1960, the _____ General Conference of Weights and Measures in France recommended an International System of Units.
e: In 1960, the Eleventh General Conference of Weights and Measures in France recommended an International System of Units. The physics in this sentence is built around Eleventh.

q: The full name of SI units is 'Systeme International d' _____.
e: The full name of SI units is 'Systeme International d' Units. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: The SI unit has _____ base units.
e: The SI unit has seven base units. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: The SI base unit for length is the _____.
e: The SI base unit for length is the metre. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: The SI base unit for mass is the _____.
e: The SI base unit for mass is the kilogram. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: The SI base unit for electric current is the _____.
e: The SI base unit for electric current is the ampere. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: The SI base unit for temperature is the _____.
e: The SI base unit for temperature is the kelvin. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: The SI base unit for amount of substance is the _____.
e: The SI base unit for amount of substance is the mole. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: The SI base unit for luminous intensity is the _____.
e: The SI base unit for luminous intensity is the lumen. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: Prefixes are multiples or sub-multiples of _____.
e: Prefixes are multiples or sub-multiples of 10. The physics in this sentence is built around 10.

q: The symbol for the prefix 'femto' is _____.
e: The symbol for the prefix 'femto' is f. The physics in this sentence is built around f.

q: The factor for the prefix 'pico' is _____.
e: The factor for the prefix 'pico' is $10^{-12}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $10^{-12}$.

q: The factor for the prefix 'nano' is _____.
e: The factor for the prefix 'nano' is $10^{-9}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $10^{-9}$.

q: The symbol for the prefix 'micro' is _____.
e: The symbol for the prefix 'micro' is u. The physics in this sentence is built around u.

q: The factor for the prefix 'milli' is _____.
e: The factor for the prefix 'milli' is $10^{-3}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $10^{-3}$.

q: The factor for the prefix 'centi' is _____.
e: The factor for the prefix 'centi' is $10^{-2}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $10^{-2}$.

q: The factor for the prefix 'deci' is _____.
e: The factor for the prefix 'deci' is $10^{-1}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $10^{-1}$.

q: The symbol for the prefix 'deca' is _____.
e: The symbol for the prefix 'deca' is da. The physics in this sentence is built around da.

q: The factor for the prefix 'hecto' is _____.
e: The factor for the prefix 'hecto' is $10^{2}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $10^{2}$.

q: The symbol for the prefix 'kilo' is _____.
e: The symbol for the prefix 'kilo' is k. The physics in this sentence is built around k.

q: The factor for the prefix 'mega' is _____.
e: The factor for the prefix 'mega' is $10^{6}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $10^{6}$.

q: The factor for the prefix 'giga' is _____.
e: The factor for the prefix 'giga' is $10^{9}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $10^{9}$.

q: The symbol for the prefix 'tera' is _____.
e: The symbol for the prefix 'tera' is G. The physics in this sentence is built around G.

q: In scientific notation, the decimal point is placed after the first _____ digit.
e: In scientific notation, the decimal point is placed after the first nonzero digit. The physics in this sentence is built around nonzero.

q: In scientific notation, if we moved the decimal point to the left, the power of 10 is _____.
e: In scientific notation, if we moved the decimal point to the left, the power of 10 is positive. The physics in this sentence is built around positive.

q: In scientific notation, if we moved the decimal point to the right, the power of 10 is _____.
e: In scientific notation, if we moved the decimal point to the right, the power of 10 is negative. The physics in this sentence is built around negative.

q: The standard of length is _____.
e: The standard of length is metre. The physics in this sentence is built around metre involving length.

q: The metre was originally defined as the length between two marks on a platinum-iridium rod at _____, kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures at Sevres, near Paris.
e: The metre was originally defined as the length between two marks on a platinum-iridium rod at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$, kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures at Sevres, near Paris. By definition that quantity is $0^{\circ}\text{C}$.

q: Nowadays the standard of length used is based on the wavelength of orange-red light emitted by a _____ isotope.
e: Nowadays the standard of length used is based on the wavelength of orange-red light emitted by a krypton 86 isotope. Wavelength is crest to next crest, and v equals f lambda involving used.

q: A metre is now defined as the length equivalent to _____ times the wavelength of orange-red light emitted by a krypton 86 isotope.
e: A metre is now defined as the length equivalent to $1\,650\,763.73$ times the wavelength of orange-red light emitted by a krypton 86 isotope. Wavelength is crest to next crest, and v equals f lambda.

q: In 1983, the metre was given a new operational definition based on the speed of _____.
e: In 1983, the metre was given a new operational definition based on the speed of light. The physics in this sentence is built around light.

q: The metre is the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of _____ of a second.
e: The metre is the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of $1/299\,792\,458$ of a second. The physics in this sentence is built around $1/299\,792\,458$.

q: In the CGS system the unit of length is the centimetre (cm) and $1 ext{ cm} = $ _____.
e: In the CGS system the unit of length is the centimetre (cm) and $1 ext{ cm} = $ $10^{-2}\text{ m}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $10^{-2}\text{ m}$.

q: In the FPS system the unit of length is the foot (ft) and $1 ext{ ft} = $ _____.
e: In the FPS system the unit of length is the foot (ft) and $1 ext{ ft} = $ $0.3048\text{ m}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $0.3048\text{ m}$.

q: The unit of length used by particle physicists is the 'Fermi' or 'femtometre' (fm) given by $1 ext{ fm} = $ _____.
e: The unit of length used by particle physicists is the 'Fermi' or 'femtometre' (fm) given by $1 ext{ fm} = $ $10^{-15}\text{ m}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $10^{-15}\text{ m}$.

q: In the field of optics, physicists use the unit angstrom ($ ext{\AA}$), where $1 ext{ \AA} = $ _____.
e: In the field of optics, physicists use the unit angstrom ($ ext{\AA}$), where $1 ext{ \AA} = $ $10^{-10}\text{ m}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $10^{-10}\text{ m}$.

q: In astronomy, the most suitable units are the astronomical unit (AU) and the _____ unit (ly).
e: In astronomy, the most suitable units are the astronomical unit (AU) and the light year unit (ly). The physics in this sentence is built around light year.

q: The light year is the distance which light travels in _____.
e: The light year is the distance which light travels in one year. The physics in this sentence is built around one year involving which.

q: The value of $1 ext{ AU}$ is equal to _____.
e: The value of $1 ext{ AU}$ is equal to $9.461 \times 10^{15}\text{ m}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $9.461 \times 10^{15}\text{ m}$.

q: The value of $1 ext{ ly}$ is equal to _____.
e: The value of $1 ext{ ly}$ is equal to $1.496 \times 10^{11}\text{ m}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $1.496 \times 10^{11}\text{ m}$.

q: The largest unit of length is the _____.
e: The largest unit of length is the parsec. The unit that belongs with this quantity is parsec.

q: The value of $1 ext{ pc}$ is equal to _____.
e: The value of $1 ext{ pc}$ is equal to $3.084 \times 10^{16}\text{ m}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $3.084 \times 10^{16}\text{ m}$.

q: The standard of mass is a cylinder of $1 ext{ kg}$ mass made of _____ alloy.
e: The standard of mass is a cylinder of $1 ext{ kg}$ mass made of platinum-iridium alloy. The physics in this sentence is built around platinum-iridium.

q: The standard kilogram is kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures at _____, near Paris.
e: The standard kilogram is kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures at Lyon, near Paris. The physics in this sentence is built around Lyon.

q: The SI base unit of time is the _____.
e: The SI base unit of time is the hour. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: The second was originally defined as $1/(60 imes 60 imes 24)$ of a _____.
e: The second was originally defined as $1/(60 imes 60 imes 24)$ of a day. By definition that quantity is day.

q: For accuracy, the second is now defined in terms of the frequency of oscillation which can occur from a _____ atom.
e: For accuracy, the second is now defined in terms of the frequency of oscillation which can occur from a krypton atom. Frequency counts complete waves per second, and v equals f lambda.

q: A particular frequency of _____ $ ext{s}^{-1}$ emitted or absorbed by a cesium atom is used to define $1 ext{ s}$.
e: A particular frequency of $9\,192\,631\,770$ $ ext{s}^{-1}$ emitted or absorbed by a cesium atom is used to define $1 ext{ s}$. Frequency counts complete waves per second, and v equals f lambda.

q: For everyday use, the standard for measuring length may be a yard stick, ruler, _____ and so on.
e: For everyday use, the standard for measuring length may be a yard stick, ruler, metre stick and so on. The physics in this sentence is built around metre stick.

q: Lengths are usually measured in metre, centimetre or _____.
e: Lengths are usually measured in metre, centimetre or millimetre. The physics in this sentence is built around millimetre involving metre.

q: Greater lengths are measured in _____.
e: Greater lengths are measured in kilometre. The physics in this sentence is built around kilometre involving measured.

q: For measuring several metres (m), the suitable instrument is a _____.
e: For measuring several metres (m), the suitable instrument is a measuring tape. The physics in this sentence is built around measuring tape.

q: The accuracy of a measuring tape is _____.
e: The accuracy of a measuring tape is $1\text{ mm} (= 0.1\text{ cm})$. The physics in this sentence is built around $1\text{ mm} (= 0.1\text{ cm})$.

q: For measuring several centimetres (cm) to $1 ext{ m}$, the suitable instrument is a metre rule or _____.
e: For measuring several centimetres (cm) to $1 ext{ m}$, the suitable instrument is a metre rule or half-metre rule. The physics in this sentence is built around half-metre rule.

q: For measuring between $1 ext{ cm}$ and $10 ext{ cm}$, the suitable instrument is _____.
e: For measuring between $1 ext{ cm}$ and $10 ext{ cm}$, the suitable instrument is Vernier calipers. The physics in this sentence is built around Vernier calipers.

q: The accuracy of Vernier calipers is _____.
e: The accuracy of Vernier calipers is $0.1\text{ mm} (= 0.01\text{ cm})$. The physics in this sentence is built around $0.1\text{ mm} (= 0.01\text{ cm})$.

q: For measuring less than $2 ext{ cm}$, the suitable instrument is a screw gauge or _____.
e: For measuring less than $2 ext{ cm}$, the suitable instrument is a screw gauge or Micrometer. The physics in this sentence is built around Micrometer.

q: The accuracy of a screw gauge (Micrometer) is _____.
e: The accuracy of a screw gauge (Micrometer) is $0.01\text{ mm} (= 0.001\text{ cm})$. The physics in this sentence is built around $0.01\text{ mm} (= 0.001\text{ cm})$.

q: The mass of an object is a measure of the amount of _____ in it.
e: The mass of an object is a measure of the amount of matter in it. Matter here means anything that has mass and occupies space. Weight: the gravitational pull of the Earth on a body, a downward force.

q: Mass is measured in laboratories using a sliding mass balance or the _____.
e: Mass is measured in laboratories using a sliding mass balance or the Vernier calipers. The physics in this sentence is built around Vernier calipers.

q: The _____ balance is easier to use and also more accurate than sliding mass balance.
e: The electronic balance is easier to use and also more accurate than sliding mass balance. The physics in this sentence is built around electronic.

q: The balance really detects the gravitational pull on the object (weight), but the scale is marked to show the _____.
e: The balance really detects the gravitational pull on the object (weight), but the scale is marked to show the density. Density here means mass per unit volume.

q: The mass of purified drinking water of 1 litre bottle is _____.
e: The mass of purified drinking water of 1 litre bottle is $1\text{ kg}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $1\text{ kg}$.

q: Time is measured in years, months, days, hours, minutes and seconds, but the SI unit for time is the _____.
e: Time is measured in years, months, days, hours, minutes and seconds, but the SI unit for time is the second (s). SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit involving months.

q: Most common modern clocks and watches depend on the vibration of _____ crystals to keep time accurately.
e: Most common modern clocks and watches depend on the vibration of quartz crystals to keep time accurately. The physics in this sentence is built around quartz.

q: The energy to keep quartz crystals vibrating comes from a small _____.
e: The energy to keep quartz crystals vibrating comes from a small battery. The physics in this sentence is built around battery.

q: A stopwatch or a stop clock can be chosen to measure the time to an accuracy of a few _____ of a second.
e: A stopwatch or a stop clock can be chosen to measure the time to an accuracy of a few tenths of a second. The physics in this sentence is built around tenths.

q: Digital stopwatches can measure up to an accuracy of _____.
e: Digital stopwatches can measure up to an accuracy of $0.01\text{ s}$. The physics in this sentence is built around $0.01\text{ s}$.
